records.contract_purpose: A small ETH-donation forwarder. A payable entry point (selector 0x7fb74289) accepts ETH and immediately forwards the received value to a single hardcoded address; two other entry points (0x4576d251, 0xb9635e63) appear to be simple read-only getters. No decompiler-resolved name was found for any of the 3 selectors (not in the 4byte.directory database), but the forwarding behavior itself is directly readable in the bytecode.
records.access_control_analysis: No caller restriction was found anywhere in the bytecode (CALLER is used only inside event-emission code, never in a comparison/JUMPI). This appears to be by design: it is a public donation-forwarding function, not a privileged one.
records.initialization_analysis: No initializer or constructor-style setup function was identified in the runtime bytecode.
records.proxy_and_upgrade_analysis: Not a proxy. No DELEGATECALL present.
records.asset_operation_analysis: Forwards CALLVALUE (ETH the caller sends in the same transaction) to the fixed address 0x88adce4c2acb8d0e047f4135ff0d313dd4972552. It does not touch any pre-existing balance or token approvals of the account.
records.authorization_specific_analysis: Self-call / tx.origin authorization pattern discussed in access_control_analysis and concrete_finding (Pilot items were hand-traced; see relevant_code_snippet in Pilot_Code_Review.xlsx for the exact guard opcode sequence).
records.concrete_finding: The only asset movement is of ETH the caller explicitly sends in the same call, redirected to one fixed, hardcoded destination. There is no mechanism found to move the account's pre-existing balance or approvals. If used as an EIP-7702 delegate, any ETH sent to the account with this selector would be redirected to the fixed donor address rather than kept by the account -- a real, describable behavior, but not a theft of existing assets.
records.unresolved_questions: The exact purpose of the two unnamed view selectors (0x4576d251, 0xb9635e63) was not determined -- 4byte.directory has no matching signature for either.

records.contract_purpose: A proxy contract in the Safe (formerly Gnosis Safe) proxy pattern: it exposes masterCopy() and setup(...) directly, and forwards every other call via DELEGATECALL to a singleton implementation address read from storage slot 0.
records.sensitive_functions: setup(address[],uint256,address,bytes,address,address,uint256,address) [0xb63e800d]; masterCopy() [0xa619486e, fallback-dispatched]; fallback DELEGATECALL to slot-0 address
records.access_control_analysis: setup() can only succeed if the caller supplies calldata that hashes to one specific pre-committed value -- it cannot be used to point the proxy at an attacker-chosen implementation, because the implementation address it writes is a fixed constant, not derived from the caller's input. All other functionality passes through to the resolved implementation contract.
records.initialization_analysis: setup() is effectively a one-shot, hash-gated initializer that pins the proxy to its singleton. It does not take the implementation address as a parameter, so it cannot be redirected.
records.proxy_and_upgrade_analysis: Confirmed DELEGATECALL proxy. Implementation resolved on-chain (storage slot 0) to 0xcfaa26ad40bfc7e3b1642e1888620fc402b95dab, a 22,528-byte unverified contract whose full decompiled selector set is an EXACT match to the Safe (Gnosis Safe) multisig wallet's core interface: execTransaction, checkSignatures/checkNSignatures, addOwnerWithThreshold, removeOwner, swapOwner, changeThreshold, enableModule/disableModule, execTransactionFromModule, approveHash, getOwners, getThreshold, nonce, domainSeparator, getTransactionHash, setGuard, VERSION -- the complete, well-known Safe function surface. No EIP-1967 standard proxy slot is used (this is Safe's own legacy slot-0 convention), and the implementation address cannot be changed by any function found in this proxy's own bytecode.
records.asset_operation_analysis: Any asset movement happens inside the (unverified) implementation contract via execTransaction()/execTransactionFromModule(), which is the standard Safe multisig-signature-gated transaction path -- not directly inspectable without full source, but structurally identical to Safe's well-audited design.
records.authorization_specific_analysis: Self-call / tx.origin authorization pattern discussed in access_control_analysis and concrete_finding (Pilot items were hand-traced; see relevant_code_snippet in Pilot_Code_Review.xlsx for the exact guard opcode sequence).
records.concrete_finding: The proxy itself cannot be redirected to an attacker-controlled implementation. The resolved implementation's function selector set is identical to genuine Safe -- a heavily audited, extremely widely deployed (many billions of dollars secured) multisig implementation. This was not verified as byte-identical to a specific published Safe release (unverified on Sourcify/Blockscout at this non-canonical address), so a subtly modified fork cannot be fully ruled out from selectors alone.
records.evidence_references: pilot_code_evidence/polygon_0x32ab10ebca6121659e41d7caa364147d87ebd74e/decompiled/ (disassembly.txt offsets 0-263, functions.json); implementation resolved on-chain via eth_getStorageAt(slot 0) -> 0xcfaa26ad40bfc7e3b1642e1888620fc402b95dab, decompiled separately at pilot_code_evidence/_shared_implementations/0xcfaa26ad40bfc7e3b1642e1888620fc402b95dab/
records.unresolved_questions: Whether the resolved implementation (0xcfaa26ad40bfc7e3b1642e1888620fc402b95dab) is byte-for-byte identical to an official Safe release, or a modified fork with the same external interface, was not established -- no verified source was available for it either.

records.contract_purpose: A restricted call-forwarding router. Exposes forward(address,bytes) which relays a call (with any ETH sent) to a caller-supplied target, but only for one specific, hardcoded authorized address.
records.access_control_analysis: forward() is gated by an exact-match check: require(msg.sender == 0xe51504ffee530eaf61f6af654793ce459ff98833). This is a fixed, non-upgradeable single-caller restriction -- confirmed directly in the bytecode, not inferred from selector names.
records.initialization_analysis: No initializer found; the authorized-caller address is a hardcoded constant, not stored/settable state.
records.proxy_and_upgrade_analysis: Not a proxy. No DELEGATECALL present.
records.asset_operation_analysis: forward() can direct an arbitrary CALL (any target, any calldata, any ETH received in the same transaction) -- but only when triggered by the one hardcoded authorized address.
records.authorization_specific_analysis: Self-call / tx.origin authorization pattern discussed in access_control_analysis and concrete_finding (Pilot items were hand-traced; see relevant_code_snippet in Pilot_Code_Review.xlsx for the exact guard opcode sequence).
records.concrete_finding: The arbitrary-call capability is real, but it is not reachable by an arbitrary caller: only 0xe51504ffee530eaf61f6af654793ce459ff98833 can invoke it, confirmed by an exact CALLER comparison at the very start of the function body.
records.unresolved_questions: The identity/nature of the hardcoded authorized address (0xe51504ffee530eaf61f6af654793ce459ff98833) -- e.g. whether it is an EOA the account owner controls, or some other operator -- was not determined from bytecode alone.

records.contract_purpose: A large, stateful contract exposing a full OpenZeppelin-style Ownable access-control surface (owner, transferOwnership, renounceOwnership) plus custom functions coin(), burn(), initialize(address,address[]), drain(uint256), and dust() -- consistent with an owner-controlled wallet/vault that also references an external ERC-20 token ('coin').
records.sensitive_functions: drain(uint256) [0xf6b19c74]; dust() [0xfad9aba3]; burn() [0x44df8e70]; transferOwnership(address) [0xf2fde38b]; renounceOwnership() [0x715018a6]; initialize(address,address[]) [0x946d9204]
records.access_control_analysis: The presence of OZ Ownable's exact custom-error-construction pattern (rather than just the owner()/transferOwnership() selector names) is strong, specific evidence that this contract uses the real, standard onlyOwner modifier -- not merely a contract that happens to expose similarly-named functions.
records.initialization_analysis: initialize(address,address[]) exists as a separate function from owner assignment. Whether it can be called more than once, or by an unauthorized party, was NOT traced within this review's scope -- flagged as an open question.
records.proxy_and_upgrade_analysis: Not a proxy. No DELEGATECALL present.
records.asset_operation_analysis: drain(uint256), dust(), and burn() all move value; transferFrom/approve selectors (per the earlier structural scan) suggest interaction with an external ERC-20 ('coin'). Given the confirmed Ownable pattern, these are very likely all behind the same onlyOwner check, though each individual call site was not traced one by one.
records.authorization_specific_analysis: Self-call / tx.origin authorization pattern discussed in access_control_analysis and concrete_finding (Pilot items were hand-traced; see relevant_code_snippet in Pilot_Code_Review.xlsx for the exact guard opcode sequence).
records.concrete_finding: Strong, specific evidence (the literal OZ Ownable custom-error construction, not just selector names) supports that sensitive functions are gated to the account's owner.
records.evidence_references: pilot_code_evidence/ethereum_0xd24558a256c4aa2d0b6c3a7e12b2f70f810e7b04/decompiled/ (disassembly.txt offsets 3400-3470, 5470-5560; functions.json lists all 12 dispatched + 15 resolved fallback/error selectors including OwnableUnauthorizedAccount-style Panic/Error selectors)
records.unresolved_questions: Whether initialize(address,address[]) has a single-use guard (e.g. an OZ Initializable pattern) was not confirmed -- this is the standard 'can initialization be front-run or repeated' question and was not traced for this specific function within this review's scope.

records.contract_purpose: A single-function contract (selector 0x040113fc, unnamed in 4byte.directory) that appears to perform an authorized action gated by a tx.origin check against one hardcoded address.
records.access_control_analysis: The guard uses the ORIGIN opcode (tx.origin), not CALLER (msg.sender). This is the well-known SWC-115 'Authorization through tx.origin' anti-pattern: if the address 0x9dcb4c...54caa (likely the account owner's EOA) ever interacts with any malicious contract while this delegate is authorized, that malicious contract could call into this function on the victim's behalf and pass the tx.origin check, because tx.origin does not change across a chain of contract calls the way msg.sender does.
records.initialization_analysis: No initializer found; the authorized address is a hardcoded constant.
records.proxy_and_upgrade_analysis: Not a proxy. No DELEGATECALL present.
records.asset_operation_analysis: Not fully traced beyond the guard itself; no token-transfer or approval selector was detected structurally.
records.authorization_specific_analysis: Self-call / tx.origin authorization pattern discussed in access_control_analysis and concrete_finding (Pilot items were hand-traced; see relevant_code_snippet in Pilot_Code_Review.xlsx for the exact guard opcode sequence).
records.concrete_finding: Concrete, well-documented anti-pattern: authorization via tx.origin (SWC-115) rather than msg.sender, phishable via a malicious intermediate contract regardless of what the specific hardcoded address is.
records.unresolved_questions: What action this function actually performs once the tx.origin check passes was not fully traced (beyond the guard itself).

records.contract_purpose: A stateful contract exposing transferTokens(address) and executeCall(address,bytes), both of which move value/perform arbitrary calls, plus two unnamed selectors.
records.access_control_analysis: No caller-identity check of any kind (msg.sender or tx.origin) exists anywhere in this contract's bytecode. This was confirmed by scanning the complete disassembly, not a truncated prefix -- the absence is a hard fact about the whole program, not an inference from limited visibility.
records.initialization_analysis: No initializer found.
records.proxy_and_upgrade_analysis: Not a proxy. No DELEGATECALL present.
records.asset_operation_analysis: transferTokens(address) and executeCall(address,bytes) both appear payable and, absent any caller check, are reachable by anyone.
records.authorization_specific_analysis: Self-call / tx.origin authorization pattern discussed in access_control_analysis and concrete_finding (Pilot items were hand-traced; see relevant_code_snippet in Pilot_Code_Review.xlsx for the exact guard opcode sequence).
records.concrete_finding: transferTokens() and executeCall() -- an arbitrary-call function -- have no caller restriction anywhere in the contract. If this is the account's active EIP-7702 delegate, anyone could invoke executeCall() to make the account perform an arbitrary call (potentially moving assets, granting approvals, or anything else the account's balance/permissions allow).
records.unresolved_questions: The two unnamed selectors (0x29cd3d04, 0x535089e7) were not individually characterized beyond confirming they too are reachable without any caller check.

records.contract_purpose: A single-controller executor. A plain ETH transfer (no calldata) is forwarded in full to one hardcoded address; the one dispatched function, start(address[],uint256[]), is restricted to that same address and appears to perform a batch token transfer(address,uint256) loop.
records.access_control_analysis: start() is gated by an exact match: require(msg.sender == 0xbb7218d77f06a89c15e9188b1f1b427ae8f0290c) -- the same address that receives forwarded ETH. This is a single, fixed, non-upgradeable controller/beneficiary design.
records.initialization_analysis: No initializer found; the controller address is a hardcoded constant.
records.proxy_and_upgrade_analysis: Not a proxy. No DELEGATECALL present.
records.asset_operation_analysis: start() appears to loop over the given address/amount arrays performing transfer(address,uint256)-style calls (per the fallback-candidate selector list), reachable only by the fixed controller address.
records.authorization_specific_analysis: Self-call / tx.origin authorization pattern discussed in access_control_analysis and concrete_finding (Pilot items were hand-traced; see relevant_code_snippet in Pilot_Code_Review.xlsx for the exact guard opcode sequence).
records.concrete_finding: Both the ETH-forwarding fallback and the batch-transfer function converge on the same single, fixed address -- a consistent, coherent single-controller design with a confirmed caller check, not an open function.

records.contract_purpose: A minimal value-forwarding contract exposing destination() (a getter for a stored address) and one other function (0xcf641220) that forwards value to that stored destination.
records.sensitive_functions: destination() [0xb269681d, view]; 0xcf641220 (nonpayable, likely the transfer trigger)
records.access_control_analysis: No CALLER or ORIGIN opcode was found anywhere in this contract's full 2,175-instruction disassembly -- confirmed by an exhaustive scan. The transfer-triggering function (0xcf641220) has no caller restriction.
records.initialization_analysis: No initializer found; storage_operations recorded exactly 1 SSTORE somewhere in the program, but the code path that performs it was not located within this review's scope -- it may be a constructor-only write not present in runtime code, or a runtime setter not yet traced.
records.proxy_and_upgrade_analysis: Not a proxy. No DELEGATECALL present.
records.asset_operation_analysis: The 0xcf641220 function appears to trigger sending value to the stored 'destination' address, callable by anyone (no caller check found).
records.authorization_specific_analysis: Self-call / tx.origin authorization pattern discussed in access_control_analysis and concrete_finding (Pilot items were hand-traced; see relevant_code_snippet in Pilot_Code_Review.xlsx for the exact guard opcode sequence).
records.concrete_finding: Unlike the items above with unrestricted arbitrary-call capability, this function's target is fixed (the stored 'destination', not attacker-supplied per-call) -- so an open caller does not translate into an open destination. Whether 'destination' itself can be changed by an unauthorized party was not conclusively established.
records.unresolved_questions: Whether 'destination' can be set/changed at runtime by an arbitrary caller (the single SSTORE's guard was not located) is the key open question -- if it can, this would be a more serious finding; if 'destination' is fixed at deploy time, this is a low-risk, if unrestricted, forwarding utility.

records.contract_purpose: A batch-executor smart-account-style contract. owner() and a self-address getter (0x773d5602) are both exposed; the batch-execute function (0x04f3a55d) is gated to the owner or the contract itself; a plain ETH transfer is forwarded to the owner with a 2300-gas stipend.
records.access_control_analysis: require(msg.sender == owner || msg.sender == address(this)) -- a standard, appropriate 'owner-or-self' guard consistent with an EIP-7702 smart-account design (the 'self' branch allows the account to call its own batch-executor internally, e.g. from a multicall or session-key wrapper).
records.initialization_analysis: No separate initializer found; owner is a fixed constant (0xe039802366498c5cc75b200decaa9ad520e60a11) baked into the bytecode.
records.proxy_and_upgrade_analysis: Not a proxy. No DELEGATECALL present.
records.asset_operation_analysis: The batch executor can perform arbitrary calls (with value), but only when triggered by the owner or the account itself.
records.authorization_specific_analysis: Self-call / tx.origin authorization pattern discussed in access_control_analysis and concrete_finding (Pilot items were hand-traced; see relevant_code_snippet in Pilot_Code_Review.xlsx for the exact guard opcode sequence).
records.concrete_finding: A concrete, appropriate dual-caller guard (owner OR self) protects the only capability found that could move assets or make arbitrary calls.
records.unresolved_questions: None material to the SAFE/UNSAFE decision; the owner address's own trustworthiness is outside this review's scope (it is presumed to be the account holder).

records.contract_purpose: A contract with a self-destruct capability, gated by a tx.origin check, plus a 'sweep remaining balance' style utility.
records.access_control_analysis: Both the SELFDESTRUCT-reaching function and the other gated function use ORIGIN (tx.origin), not CALLER (msg.sender), for their authorization check. This is the SWC-115 'Authorization through tx.origin' anti-pattern -- confirmed directly, not inferred.
records.initialization_analysis: No initializer found; the authorized address is a hardcoded constant.
records.proxy_and_upgrade_analysis: Not a proxy. No DELEGATECALL present.
records.asset_operation_analysis: The 0x0a7c8ed6 function appears to sweep the contract's own balance (SELFBALANCE-gated CALL pattern) to the authorized address; destroyMe() self-destructs the contract.
records.authorization_specific_analysis: Self-call / tx.origin authorization pattern discussed in access_control_analysis and concrete_finding (Pilot items were hand-traced; see relevant_code_snippet in Pilot_Code_Review.xlsx for the exact guard opcode sequence).
records.concrete_finding: HIGH PRIORITY, concrete finding: the ability to permanently self-destruct this contract's code is gated only by a tx.origin check against a fixed address. If that address (likely the account owner) ever interacts with any malicious contract while this delegate is authorized, the malicious contract could trigger destroyMe() on the victim's behalf via the classic tx.origin phishing vector, since tx.origin persists across the whole call chain regardless of msg.sender.
records.unresolved_questions: None material -- the vulnerability class itself (tx.origin auth on a SELFDESTRUCT path) is sufficient grounds for concern regardless of the specific hardcoded address's identity.

records.contract_purpose: A large (9,874-byte), sophisticated contract using OpenZeppelin's Initializable + AccessControl (role-based permissions) libraries, plus ERC-1271 signature validation (isValidSignature) and an ERC-4337-style createSender(bytes) function -- consistent with account-abstraction / smart-account infrastructure.
